message.content:
With RF2, every block has two copies on different nodes. When one of three nodes fails, blocks with a copy on that node are left with a single copy. Blocks whose two copies were on the surviving nodes are unaffected. The cluster stays online because the two surviving nodes still form a majority for metadata and cluster-management quorum. VMs that were running on the failed node are restarted on the remaining nodes by HA. New writes still get two copies, one on each surviving node.

The cluster does not wait for the node to be repaired. Curator finds the under-replicated data and rebuilds the missing copies across the two surviving nodes, provided they have enough free capacity. Once that finishes, the data is back at RF2.

That does not restore full fault tolerance. A two-node remainder cannot survive another node loss, because quorum would be lost and the cluster would go offline. Normal resilience returns only when the failed node is repaired or replaced.

members.label: Response D
members.answer:
With RF2, every piece of data has two copies on different nodes. When one node in a three-node cluster fails, data whose second copy lived on that node drops to a single copy. The cluster stays online and VMs keep running, since the surviving copy is still readable, but it is temporarily exposed: a second disk or node loss during this window could cause data unavailability.

The cluster does not wait for a repair. Curator detects the under-replicated extents and immediately starts rebuilding a second copy onto the two surviving nodes. Because both remaining nodes participate, this self-healing runs in parallel across the cluster. Once complete, RF2 redundancy is fully restored, provided the surviving nodes have enough free capacity to hold the extra copies.

What the cluster cannot do is tolerate another failure until that rebuild finishes. VMs on the failed node are restarted via HA on the remaining nodes. Three nodes is the minimum for RF2, so the cluster cannot lose the failed node permanently and remain fully protected without replacing it.

members.label: Response C
members.answer:
RF2 means the cluster normally keeps two copies of each data block on different nodes. When one node fails, **data remains accessible**, but blocks that had a copy on the failed node are temporarily left with only one surviving copy. Blocks whose copies were on the two surviving nodes still have both.

The cluster can continue serving reads and writes and, after declaring the node failed, can **rebuild missing data replicas across the two surviving nodes**, provided sufficient free storage capacity is available. It does not necessarily have to wait for the failed node to return to restore two copies of the user data.

However, restoring those copies does **not** make the two-node remainder tolerant of another node failure. Metadata and cluster-management quorum requirements still matter; another node loss can make the cluster unavailable. Restoring or replacing the failed node is therefore necessary to regain normal protection against a further node failure.

members.label: Response B
members.answer:
In a three-node Nutanix cluster with Replication Factor 2 (RF2), two copies of all data exist across the nodes. When one node fails, the cluster remains operational because the cluster's metadata services maintain a quorum with the two surviving nodes.

Immediately after the failure, data redundancy is temporarily compromised. Any data blocks that had one of their replicas on the failed node drop to RF1 (a single copy), meaning they exist only on one of the surviving nodes.

To resolve this, the cluster automatically initiates a self-healing rebuild process. Background services identify the under-replicated data and recreate the missing copies on the remaining two nodes. As long as there is sufficient free storage capacity, the cluster will successfully restore data redundancy back to RF2. 

However, despite data redundancy being restored, the cluster's overall resilience is degraded. With only two nodes remaining, the metadata quorum cannot tolerate a second node failure without bringing the entire cluster offline.

members.label: Response A
members.answer:
In a Nutanix AOS cluster that is configured with **RF 2 (Replication Factor 2)**, every data block is stored on two separate nodes. If one of the three nodes fails, the cluster instantly loses the *second* copy for the blocks whose replicas were on that node.  

The cluster therefore operates with **reduced redundancy**: those blocks now exist on only a single node, while the rest of the data still has two copies. Because Nutanix’s distributed architecture maintains quorum with a majority of nodes, the cluster remains **fully functional**—VMs, apps, and services continue to run and data can still be read and written (writes will be placed on the surviving replica).

Immediately after the failure the cluster’s self‑healing process kicks in. It **re‑replicates** the affected blocks onto the remaining nodes (or onto any newly added replacement node) to restore RF 2 for the whole datastore. Until this rebuild finishes, the cluster is vulnerable: a second node loss would cause permanent data loss for any blocks that have not yet been re‑replicated. Once the rebuild finishes, full redundancy and fault‑tolerance are re‑established.
